characterized_levers.name: Technical Feasibility Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy. Immediate: Demonstrators built → Systemic: 15% increased policy traction due to concrete evidence → Strategic: Enhanced credibility in procurement negotiations.
options: Focus demonstrator efforts on a single, highly secure authentication method, such as FIDO2, on a mainstream Android device.
Develop demonstrators for both FIDO2 on GrapheneOS and a browser-based fallback, accepting slightly longer development timelines.
Explore passwordless authentication via blockchain-anchored identity and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) alongside FIDO2 and browser-based fallback demonstrators.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Technical Risk vs. Scope. Weakness: The options don't explicitly address the cost implications of each demonstrator approach.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on demonstrating technical feasibility to impact policy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of the technical demonstrators on policy traction, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to demonstrator development.
characterized_levers.description: Technical Feasibility Strategy aims to demonstrate the technical viability of a platform-neutral and fallback-capable Danish digital identity system. It controls the risk associated with developing demonstrators that showcase secure authentication methods, such as FIDO2 on GrapheneOS or browser-based fallbacks. The objective is to provide concrete evidence that can enhance credibility in procurement negotiations and inform policy decisions.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Technical Feasibility Strategy has strong synergy with Policy Advocacy Strategy, as demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy traction. By providing concrete evidence of secure authentication methods, Technical Feasibility Strategy amplifies the advocacy efforts of Policy Advocacy Strategy, increasing the likelihood of influencing AltID requirements and adoption of platform-neutral standards.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Technical Feasibility Strategy conflicts with Coalition Building Strategy in terms of speed vs. breadth of support. While building a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders might accelerate progress, it may not provide the same level of systemic impact as expanding the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.

characterized_levers.name: Policy Advocacy Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Policy advocacy shapes procurement. Immediate: Policy proposals submitted → Systemic: 20% greater likelihood of influencing AltID requirements → Strategic: Increased adoption of platform-neutral standards.
options: Focus advocacy on continuity of service and supplier concentration risks, avoiding direct privacy arguments.
Balance continuity arguments with privacy and democratic accountability concerns, broadening the coalition.
Prioritize open-source governance and community-led development models for digital identity, framing platform neutrality as a public good.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Political Risk vs. Coalition Size. Weakness: The options don't consider the potential for regulatory capture by incumbent vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on policy advocacy shaping procurement, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of policy advocacy on influencing AltID requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to advocacy focus.
characterized_levers.description: Policy Advocacy Strategy seeks to shape procurement decisions by reframing the issue of digital identity in terms of continuity of service, supplier concentration risks, and democratic accountability. It controls the risk associated with influencing policy and procurement documents to include platform-neutral language and certified fallback authentication paths.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Policy Advocacy Strategy has strong synergy with Technical Feasibility Strategy, as demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy traction. By providing concrete evidence of secure authentication methods, Policy Advocacy Strategy can leverage this evidence to increase the likelihood of influencing AltID requirements and adoption of platform-neutral standards.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Policy Advocacy Strategy conflicts with Procurement Influence Strategy in terms of specificity vs. implementability. While advocating for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths might be more effective, it may not account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.

characterized_levers.name: Coalition Building Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Coalition strength amplifies advocacy. Immediate: Stakeholder engagement increased → Systemic: 30% stronger advocacy position in procurement discussions → Strategic: Greater political pressure for platform neutrality.
options: Build a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders.
Expand the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.
Actively recruit dissenting voices from within the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to foster internal debate.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Speed vs. Breadth of Support. Weakness: The options fail to address the potential for conflicting priorities within the coalition.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on coalition building to amplify advocacy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of coalition strength on advocacy position, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to coalition composition.
characterized_levers.description: Coalition Building Strategy aims to build a strong coalition of stakeholders, including civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers. It controls the risk associated with building a broad coalition that can amplify advocacy efforts.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Coalition Building Strategy has strong synergy with Policy Advocacy Strategy, as building a strong coalition amplifies advocacy efforts. By engaging with diverse stakeholders, Coalition Building Strategy can increase the likelihood of influencing AltID requirements and adoption of platform-neutral standards.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Coalition Building Strategy conflicts with Technical Feasibility Strategy in terms of speed vs. breadth of support. While building a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders might accelerate progress, it may not provide the same level of systemic impact as expanding the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.

characterized_levers.name: Procurement Influence Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Procurement influence drives adoption. Immediate: Platform-neutral language included in procurement documents → Systemic: 25% faster scaling through mandated supplier diversity → Strategic: Reduced long-term dependency on Apple and Google.
options: Focus on including general language about supplier concentration risk in AltID procurement documents.
Advocate for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths.
Propose a 'digital sovereignty bonus' in procurement scoring, rewarding vendors who demonstrably reduce platform dependency.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Specificity vs. Implementability. Weakness: The options don't account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on procurement influence driving adoption, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of procurement influence on scaling, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to procurement language.
characterized_levers.description: Procurement Influence Strategy seeks to drive adoption by influencing procurement decisions to include platform-neutral language and certified fallback authentication paths. It controls the risk associated with shaping procurement documents and vendor behavior.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Procurement Influence Strategy has strong synergy with Policy Advocacy Strategy, as reframing the issue of digital identity in terms of continuity of service and supplier concentration risks can inform procurement decisions. By advocating for platform-neutral language and certified fallback authentication paths, Procurement Influence Strategy can increase the likelihood of influencing AltID requirements and adoption of platform-neutral standards.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Procurement Influence Strategy conflicts with Policy Advocacy Strategy in terms of specificity vs. implementability. While advocating for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths might be more effective, it may not account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.

characterized_levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: EU standards engagement creates broader impact. Immediate: Input provided to relevant EU bodies → Systemic: 10% increased alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements → Strategic: Enhanced interoperability and reduced lock-in across Europe.
options: Monitor relevant EU bodies and technical working groups, providing occasional input on interoperability.
Actively engage with EU bodies, advocating for platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms in eIDAS2 and related standards.
Champion a 'sovereign identity sandbox' within the EU Digital Identity Wallet framework to test and validate platform-neutral authentication models.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Resource Allocation vs. Scope of Influence. Weakness: The options don't address the potential for EU standards to be influenced by large platform vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on EU standards engagement creating broader impact, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of EU standards engagement on alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to EU engagement strategies.
characterized_levers.description: EU Standards Engagement Strategy seeks to create broader impact by engaging with EU bodies and technical working groups. It controls the risk associated with influencing EU standards and ensuring interoperability across Europe.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy has strong synergy with Policy Advocacy Strategy, as engaging with EU bodies can inform policy decisions and increase the likelihood of influencing AltID requirements and adoption of platform-neutral standards. By advocating for platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms in eIDAS2 and related standards, EU Standards Engagement Strategy can enhance interoperability and reduce lock-in across Europe.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy conflicts with Technical Feasibility Strategy in terms of resource allocation vs. scope of influence. While engaging with EU bodies might require significant resources, it may not provide the same level of systemic impact as demonstrating technical feasibility through demonstrators.
